```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

`attitudedyn` fits a panel of ordinal attitudes by simulated maximum likelihood, following the Nepaul and Stern (2026) replication package. Several Likert items measured on the same people over several waves share a persistence matrix and a small number of person factors. The whole latent attitude carries forward from one wave to the next.

```{r}
library(attitudedyn)
panel <- simulate_attitudes(n_persons = 40, n_waves = 3, n_factors = 1, seed = 1)
head(panel)
```

The data are in long form: one row is one person in one wave. Outcomes are integers `1, ..., K`. The cut between category 1 and category 2 is normalised at zero, so that numbering is part of the model.

```{r}
fit <- attitudedyn(
  cbind(y1, y2) ~ x,
  data = panel,
  id = ~ id,
  wave = ~ wave,
  time = ~ time,
  n_factors = 1,
  draws = 6,
  control = attitudedyn_control(maxit = 0, n_threads = 1, vcov = "none")
)
summary(fit)
```

`coef()` returns the unconstrained coefficients that the optimiser sees. Persistence coefficients are transformed to the interval (-1, 1) inside the likelihood. `persistence_matrix()` reports that scale: the row is the attitude that receives the lag, and the column is the attitude that is lagged.

```{r}
persistence_matrix(fit)
variance_decomposition(fit)
impulse_response(fit, horizon = 3)$response[, "y1", "y1"]
```
